1:
That these two should be together is what everyone notices first. Chrysostom observes that we find them everywhere in great harmony — Peter beckoning to John at the supper, the two running to the sepulchre, Peter asking afterwards, what shall this man do? Gill says the same more plainly, that they were intimate companions and great lovers of each other, thought by some to have been together in the high priest's palace at the trial. Ellicott lays out the record of the friendship: partners as fishermen, sharers in looking for the consolation of Israel, sent together to prepare the passover, and after the denial it was to John that Peter turned for comfort — so that Renan's notion, that the fourth Gospel was written to exalt its author at Peter's expense, may take its place among the morbid imaginations of inventive interpretation. Henry adds a conjecture. Each had a brother among the twelve, yet they are knit more closely to each other than to their own kin, there being a friend that sticks closer than a brother; and he supposes the reason to be that John, a disciple made up of love, was tenderer of Peter in his fall and more solicitous to restore him than any of the rest, so that Christ's favourite becoming his bosom friend was itself evidence of Peter's acceptance upon repentance.

Why they went up at all is the harder question. Barnes notes that the disciples resorted daily to the temple, that whether they joined in its sacrifices is not said, and that they came only slowly to the conclusion that they were to leave it; he adds that Luke enters into particulars where an impostor would have been content with a general claim of many wonders, a proof of honesty. Calvin will not put the visit down to the rite of the law: it is likelier they went up for the better opportunity of spreading the gospel. Nor will he let the verse be abused into a licence for joining in superstitious worship, since God himself had appointed the morning and evening sacrifice, teaching the people to begin and end the day with calling on his name; two men who came into a house consecrated to God and called on the God of Israel there polluted themselves in nothing. Robertson agrees that Peter and John, like Paul after them, kept up the Jewish worship without treating it as a means of redemption, and catches the imperfect: they were ascending the terraces to the courts.

The hour is fixed at three in the afternoon, and the reckoning behind it set out at length. Wesley explains that the twelve hours ran from sunrise to sunset and were therefore of unequal length as the days lengthened or shortened; the chief hours of prayer were the third and the ninth, when the morning and evening sacrifices were offered and incense, an emblem of prayer, was burnt on the golden altar. Calvin divides the day into four parts and takes the ninth for the last of them, whence he draws the probable conjecture that this was the hour of the evening sacrifice. Clarke reports the rabbinic ascription of the three times to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and prefers Tanchum's division, that men should pray when the sun rises, when it gains the meridian, and when it sets — adding that he should be glad to know every Christian observed the rule. Of the man himself the older voices say most. Chrysostom notes that the disease lay in the man's nature and baffled the art of medicine, that the most obstinate diseases are those born with a man, and that the calamity was such that he could not provide his own sustenance; while Cyril, reckoning the lameness at forty years, sees in the cure the fulfilment of the promise that then shall the lame man leap as an hart.
2:
The details of the case are the guarantee of the miracle. Barnes takes the lifelong lameness as proof that there was no deception: the man had always been lame, had to be carried, and was well known to those who used that entrance. He explains the begging from a world with neither hospitals nor alms-houses, where the poor depended on charity and had to be placed where many would see them — at the gates of rich men, or beside the highway; the temple entrance was the most favourable of all, since multitudes passed and men going up for religion give more freely. Clarke makes the same point: the case must have been notorious both from the long standing of the infirmity and from the man's daily exposure in so public a place, and Luke marks them to show the incontestable nature of the cure. Gill notes that the lameness came neither from disease nor from a fall but from a defect in nature, which made what followed the more extraordinary. Ellicott finds the record of duration characteristic of this writer, and thinks the minuteness of the narrative suggests the informant may have been the cripple himself; the approaches of the temple, like those of modern mosques, were thronged with the blind and the lame.

Which gate was called Beautiful nobody can say. Barnes inclines to the eastern gate called Susan, since the sequel places the crowd at Solomon's porch. Ellicott observes that no gate of this name is mentioned by any other writer, and offers two candidates with their traditions — Nicanor, so called on one account because the hand of the great enemy of Judah had been nailed to it as a trophy, and the Susa gate, named for the old connection between Judah and Persia and so massive that twenty men were needed to open or shut it. Clarke quotes Josephus to the same effect, that one gate outside the holy house was of Corinthian brass and far excelled the nine covered with gold and silver, fifty cubits high with doors of forty; though Josephus, he grants, is by no means clear. Wesley assigns it to Herod the Great, setting it between the court of the Gentiles and that of Israel, and more pompous in workmanship than those overlaid with silver and gold.

The exchange of looks is handled with care. Barnes notes that the word for fastening the eyes means to look with fixed attention, that it is one of this writer's peculiar words, used by no other in the New Testament save Paul twice, and that the command to look was meant to fix the man's attention on the source of the cure. Robertson catches the tenses: Peter fixed his eyes and invited the man to look, and the man held his own on them with great eagerness, taking the invitation for the promise of a large gift. Ellicott makes the gaze mutual — Peter read character in the man's face and discerned faith to be healed, while the man was to read in their pitying looks not only the wish to heal but the power to do it. Calvin raises the question the moment suggests, whether the apostles could work miracles as often as they pleased, and answers that they were ministers of God's power in such sort that they attempted nothing of their own motion but waited till the Lord wrought by them — which is why they healed one man and not all; the steadfast looking was itself a motion of the Spirit, without which Peter could not have spoken so surely. He draws from the man's expectation a lesson about prayer: what was given he had never dared ask, and so God often prevents us and shows himself to those who do not seek him — yet this is no excuse for sloth, since we are commanded to pray.
6:
The poverty confessed here is less simple than it looks. Gill takes it strictly, that they had no coin of either metal about them and perhaps none of their own anywhere, only what was put into their hands as a common stock; and no money might be carried in a purse into the temple at all. Ellicott presses the difficulty, since the apostles were by then stewards of the sums the community had laid at their feet: either they had none with them, or as almoners they held themselves bound to distribute what was given in trust only to members of the society. Obeying their Master's command, they had no money of their own — but they could give more than money. Barnes reads the answer as a refusal made so as to show willingness, and glosses the next phrase as such as is in my power, without any suggestion that Peter had originated it. Calvin turns the confession into a rule: every man ought to consider what the Lord has given him, since whatever store God bestows is meant as an instrument for exercising love. The opening looks at first like mockery, Peter speaking of his poverty just after raising so rare a hope; but the comparison makes the miracle the greater.

Three voices turn the verse against the papacy. Clarke observes that the popish writers, dexterous as they are at forming analogies between Peter and the pope, have attempted none here, and that even Calmet passes the saying by. He tells the story of Thomas Aquinas entering the chamber of Innocent the Fourth while large sums were counted, and the pope saying, you see the Church is no longer in an age when she can say, silver and gold have I none — to which the angelical doctor replied, true, holy father, nor can she now say to the lame man, rise up and walk. Wesley puts it in two lines: how unlike his supposed successor, and can the bishop of Rome either say or do the same? Calvin is angriest of the three, describing a ceremony of two stone cells in which the newly created pope, asked for alms in Peter's own words, casts crosses in the air with his fingers, and is then carried to the cell where the bags of money are while his attendants cry that he has dispersed and given to the poor; Satan reigns, he says, where the Word of God is so manifestly mocked.

The name is what carries the cure, and they are careful about how. Barnes takes the phrase to mean by his authority, or in virtue of power derived from him, and finds a radical difference between the Lord's miracles and the apostles': he wrought in his own name and claimed dominion over disease and death, whereas they never attempted a miracle by their own power. Calvin guards the point from the other side: there is no magical force in the sounding of the syllables, as the Jews dote about the name Jehovah, and Peter meant only to declare himself a minister and Christ the author. The added epithet he thinks deliberate, since Nazareth was the term of contempt, and Peter of set purpose named the very Jesus they had crucified, whose name was despised and to most detestable, as the promised Messiah. Ellicott makes the trust behind the words partly faith in a promise and partly the memory of powers already exercised, and observes that the Name can hardly have been new to the beggar, since a fellow at that gate had received his sight at Siloam — what made the call a test of faith being that a few weeks earlier that Name had stood on the superscription of a cross. Robertson notes that the command to walk is inchoative, begin walking and keep on — but the beggar does not budge, knowing that he cannot.
7:
The hand offered before the strength comes is what the commentators notice. Gill takes the gesture for imitation, since Peter had often seen his Master use the same action on such occasions. Barnes makes more of it: to take hold of the hand was an offer of aid, a sign that the speaker was in earnest, and an inducement to the man to make the effort himself. He turns it into a picture of God's manner in commanding men to repent and believe, since he does not leave them alone but extends help and aids their efforts, stretching out his hand to the weak and needy. Robertson puts the practical fact more bluntly, that Peter had to pull the man up onto his feet before he would try to walk at all.

The description of what followed is unusually exact, and Ellicott thinks the exactness diagnostic. He would render the first word as soles rather than feet, and observes that this term and the ankle bones alike are more or less technical, as is the verb rendered received strength, which means literally that they were consolidated — the flaccid tissues and muscles made firm and vigorous. The precision, he says, is characteristic of a medical historian. Clarke fastens instead on the timing, that the suddenness of the cure was the proof of the miracle while the walking and leaping were its evidences. Barnes agrees that strength imparted at once to feet lame from birth was full and clear proof of miraculous power.

The leaping is read as a fulfilment and as a piece of natural behaviour at the same time. Ellicott traces the order of movements: first the upward leap in the new consciousness of power, then the successful effort to stand for the first time in his life, then the beginning of walking step by step, and at last the two motions alternating, ordinary walking broken by the leaps of an exuberant joy — and so he entered with them into the court of the women, which at the hour of the evening sacrifice would be full of worshippers. He notes that the verb is a compound of the one the Greek version uses in the promise that the lame shall leap as an hart, and Clarke says the same prophecy was now fulfilled in the most literal manner, distinguishing the three acts: he walked in obedience to the command, leaped to try his limbs and convince himself the cure was real, and praised God in gratitude. Barnes finds a further proof of the miracle in the walking itself, since walking is a skill acquired by long practice and children learn it slowly — he instances Caspar Hauser, lately discovered in a German city, who had been shut up from childhood and could only stumble awkwardly when released. That this man walked at once was clear proof. Barnes adds what he thinks the most telling detail, that the praise went to God without any prompting and without a word of thanks to Peter and John, who had not pretended to restore him in their own name. Robertson notes that he kept leaping repeatedly, and came into the temple rehearsing all three new exercises together.
9:
What makes the cure unanswerable is that the witnesses knew the man. Gill points out that he had been brought there daily and had sat asking alms for years, so that he was thoroughly known, and that the people now staring at him had passed him minutes before in his old condition — a clear and indisputable point. Barnes lists the particulars as things no imposture could satisfy: the man had been afflicted from a child and was by now forty; had he been feigning, he could hardly have escaped detection all that while in so public a place; the apostles had no hand in placing him there and had never seen him, so there was no room for collusion; the man himself was convinced, and so were the people, who had had every opportunity of knowing his condition. Nor were these friends of Jesus, but men lately busy putting him to death. Clarke presses the publicity, that the miracle was wrought in the most public place and under the notice of the priests, who were best qualified to judge of it. Ellicott would render the verb as recognised, and Robertson catches the tense: they were beginning to perceive who it was.

Calvin will not let the wonder stand as an achievement. He grants a double fruit, since the healed man acknowledges the benefit of God and the people are moved so that the fame spreads; but being filled with wondering describes only a preparation, which a fuller progress had afterwards to follow. Of itself the amazement rather astonished the people than brought them to God; it was the foundation of a building still to come. From this he draws a rule: miracles by themselves breed nothing but a confused astonishment, and though God calls us to himself by showing his goodness and power in them, such is the weakness of our nature that we faint in the midway until doctrine helps us. Where none reproves it, he adds, the abuse of miracles has bred the worship of saints, since a man who acknowledges the power of God in a miracle is easily persuaded that he owes divine honour to the man who wrought it — and the same would have befallen these Jews had not the sermon that follows called them back. Wonder must therefore be joined to teaching, and the one never separated from the other.

The place they ran to has a history. Ellicott describes the portico as standing outside the temple on the east, a double row of Corinthian columns some thirty-seven feet high, which took its name from having been built in part, when the temple was raised again under Zerubbabel, from fragments of the older edifice; the people afterwards pressed Herod Agrippa to pull it down and rebuild it, but he shrank from the cost. Like the porticoes of Greek cities it was a favourite resort, facing the morning sun in winter. He adds what the two disciples must have remembered, that here the people had once taken up stones against Jesus for saying he was one with the Father — and here they were now to hear his name preached as Holy and Just. Calvin gives the same descent another way: the old temple was pulled down, but Zerubbabel and Ezra imitated it as nearly as they could contrive, and though Herod renewed the building and made it far more gorgeous, all that vain cost had not blotted the remembrance of Solomon out of the people's hearts. Robertson notes that the word for porch is the one behind the name Stoic, that the portico stood on the east of the court of the Gentiles and was so called from being built on a remnant of the ancient foundations, and that Jesus had once taught there. Clarke reads the man's clinging to them as affection for the instruments of his cure.
12:
Chrysostom notices that this address begins without a preamble, and thinks the difference deliberate. There is greater freedom of speech here than in the earlier one, not because Peter had been afraid before, but because the hearers that day were scoffers who would not have borne it and had to be secured by an opening request for attention. Here no such management was needed, since the miracle had roused everybody and they were full of fear and amazement; so the speaker begins elsewhere, by refusing the glory to be had from them — nothing being so likely to pacify hearers as to say nothing honourable about oneself. Henry sets out three things Peter saw and used: a crowd in the temple, where a wisdom more excellent than Solomon's might be heard; a people wondering, which was ground broken up and ready for the seed; and a people on the point of adoring him, which made him step in at once, as Paul did at Lystra. Robertson notes that the people looked their amazement and Peter answered the look, the address by the covenant name of Israel being conciliatory.

The disclaimer is examined closely. Ellicott points out that the pronoun stands emphatically first — why is it on us that ye gaze? — and would render the second noun as purity or devotion. The word refers, he says, to the popular theory of miracles, that God hears a man who is a worshipper of him; true enough in general, but Peter disclaims it here, since no purity of his own would have availed apart from the Name. Clarke glosses the first term as miraculous energy and the second as religious attachment to the worship of God, and notes that some copies read power for holiness, though the received word appears to be the true one. Barnes is careful about what is reproved: not the wondering, which was proper, but the fixing of their eyes on the two men as if these were the authors of the cure — an opportunity to claim a reputation, open and refused. Henry presses the point through denials — not by any might of their own, since they had no skill in physic and no virtue in their word; not by any merit, since Peter was a sinful man and Judas, who had no holiness at all, wrought miracles in Christ's name — and draws the rule that the instruments of God's favour must be respected but never idolized.

Calvin turns the reproof into an argument. He grants that no one denies power to come from God; the trouble is that men confess it in a word and then take from God his right to adorn the creature with what they have taken, so that the power of God is placed in the saints and shut up in a stone or a stock of wood as soon as the image is consecrated. Even granting they do not offend in that first article, they think they have satisfied God by leaving him the power while assigning the miracles to the godliness of saints — a childish subterfuge, since men would not run to the saints for rain or health unless they supposed some merit had earned the privilege. If the people were forbidden to look to the apostles, he concludes, much more does the Spirit draw us from calling on every petty saint. Chrysostom sets the same modesty in a longer line, since Daniel disclaimed any wisdom of his own, Joseph asked whether interpretations did not belong to God, and David ascribed the lion and the bear to the name of the Lord; and Peter, he observes, presses himself on the fathers of old lest he seem to introduce a new doctrine. Gill and Wesley give the occasion in a line apiece: the people were running together, gazing at the two men and inquiring what had happened.
13:
The opening title is read by all of them as tactics. Gill says the old epithets are retained partly to distinguish this God from the gods of the Gentiles and partly to show regard to the God of Israel, lest men preaching Christ be taken for setters forth of a strange God. Wesley says the same of its position, that it stands at the opening so that it might appear they taught no new religion inconsistent with Moses, and had no design of diverting regard from the God of Israel. Clarke turns the title into an accusation: the God they called their own had acknowledged Jesus for his Son and wrought this miracle in his name, so that by honouring the man they slew he charged the guilt of that murder home upon them. Ellicott hears in it an echo of their Master's own teaching, since the same Name had been spoken in these precincts, not improbably in this very portico, as part of his proof that the dead rise — and is heard again in support of the apostles' witness that he himself had risen.

Calvin makes the title a rule against two misuses. God gave himself this designation, he says, to distinguish himself by a mark from idols, since we cannot comprehend him in his essence, which is unseen and infinite, and he uses means that agree with our capacity; the Turks boast that they worship the maker of heaven and earth, but vanish away before they come at heaven. Nor may the phrase be stretched into a warrant for whatever worship the fathers used: Peter expressly reckons up Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, from whom true religion proceeded, whereas many later fathers grew out of kind and became unlike the first, so that the prophets had to say, walk not in the ways of your fathers. Cyril puts the formula to another use, arguing from it against the Samaritans, who receive the Law only and admit no prophets: since God tells Moses that he is the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob, this must mean of those who have being and subsistence. On the word rendered Son, Ellicott and Robertson agree that Servant is better, the term being used throughout the later chapters of Isaiah; Robertson adds that it is not the word for son at all, and that as applied to Christ it is peculiar to this book.

The charge that follows is built on contrast. Robertson notes the emphatic pronouns, ye set against that one, and a man a murderer set against the Holy and Righteous One, the verb meaning granted as a favour. Barnes traces the legal position: the first charge was blasphemy, on which the council condemned him without proof, and when Pilate would not take cognisance of it they charged sedition instead, so that neither was made out and in the eye of the law he stood innocent. That the governor was satisfied of his innocence aggravates the crime, since they urged his death against the judgment of the man before whom they had arraigned him. Clarke puts it more sharply — Pilate wished to act according to justice, and they acted contrary to justice and equity in all their forms — and finds the choice of Barabbas characteristic, since like cleaves to like and they were murderers themselves. Ellicott observes that the two titles, startling as they sounded, had been anticipated: the demoniacs used the first of Christ, the best manuscripts give Peter's own earlier confession in the same words, and Pilate with his wife had borne witness to him as Just. He notes that both words recur in the letters of the two apostles now preaching them, which is what three years of converse with such a Master had left behind; and that Barabbas is called a murderer as well as a robber by two evangelists only.
15:
The title given to the crucified is a military word turned to another use. Barnes explains that it properly denotes a leader or commander, rendered captain elsewhere; since a commander leads on to victory and is said to obtain it, the word comes to mean the cause or author of a thing, and author or giver would express the sense here, with the added implication of dominion over life. He notes the contrast with the man they preferred, a murderer who had destroyed life, so that the destroyer was demanded and the Author of life put to death. Clarke derives the word from the roots for beginning and leading: not only does all life proceed from Christ, but the life-giving influence of the religion now proclaimed came through him — he teaches the doctrine of life, leads the way men should walk, and has purchased the life enjoyed at the end of it. So the Jews, he says, preferred a son of death to the Author of life. Robertson quotes Bengel's phrase, the magnificent antithesis between asking for a murderer and killing the Prince of life, and traces the word from an adjective for what furnishes the first cause to a noun meaning the originator. Gill takes the life meant to be natural, spiritual and eternal at once, and holds the death justly laid to them, since it was at their instigation that Pilate condemned him.

The appeal to witnesses follows at once, and is tied to the miracle just wrought. Clarke observes that having performed a striking miracle in that name, the apostles at once propose themselves as witnesses of the resurrection, the miracle being an unimpeachable proof of it. Ellicott notes that Peter falls back, as in the earlier sermon, on this one attestation, and Robertson that the claim is bold, made for the whole company who had seen the risen Christ, and never denied. On the sentence that follows, Barnes explains that the name stands for the person, after the Hebrew manner, so that no efficacy is ascribed to the syllables but to the authority of the one who bears them; and he takes the word rendered perfect soundness, found nowhere else in the New Testament, to mean integrity of parts and freedom from defect. That the apostles invited the crowd to examine the man in their presence he thinks conclusive against imposture, since a deceiver would not have exposed his case to inspection.

Whose faith healed the man is disputed. Barnes decides for the apostles' faith rather than the beggar's, since there is no evidence the man believed at all, and finds in it a fulfilment of the promise that faith would remove mountains. Clarke will not settle it: the apostles may have asked this power of the Father in the name of Christ, as they had been promised they might, or the faith may have been the man's, since in the moments when they bade him look at them they may have taught him what to believe, his mind being already prepared by what he had heard of the gift of tongues. Either way, Clarke says, faith was only the means of receiving: faith always receives and never gives. Ellicott distinguishes the efficient cause from the condition of its working: the Name did not operate as a formula of incantation, but required faith in what it represented, in worker and receiver alike — and he carries the causation a step further back, since the faith in both was itself wrought by the power of Christ. Calvin thinks the question hardly worth standing on, and is struck rather by the repetition, a token of fervent affection: Peter beats the same thing in again and again because he is wholly given to setting forth the glory of Christ, such being our nature that Christ can never be so extolled that his honour remains whole to him.
17:
After so heavy a charge the address turns, and all of them notice it. Gill takes the word brethren simply, that they were so according to the flesh, and that it testifies a cordial affection. Barnes makes more of it: after proving a crime so enormous, Peter still addresses them as of the same nation and hope, which shows he was not setting himself up as more holy by nature. Men are melted to contrition, Barnes says, not by reproaches but by love. Wesley calls it a word full of courtesy and compassion, and finds a second delicacy in the phrase about the rulers, since Peter does not say our rulers but yours — the Jewish dispensation having ceased at the death of Christ, and with it the authority of its officers. Calvin explains the turn: since men cast down with despair would have refused the doctrine altogether, Peter lifts them a little. Sermons must be so tempered that they profit the hearers, for where no hope of pardon is left the terror of punishment only hardens men — as David says, we fear the Lord when we perceive that he is easy to be pacified.

How much the plea of ignorance covers is examined closely. Barnes denies that it makes them innocent; the offence was mitigated but not removed, since they had demanded the death of a man declared innocent, urged on by fury and malice, so that the crime of murder remained. He thinks it implied that had they killed him knowing him to be the Messiah there would have been no forgiveness; and of the rulers he grants that their minds had been prejudiced by the expectation of a prince and a conqueror. Clarke calls the plea a tender and a necessary excuse, since if the whole had been done in absolute malice, with full knowledge of the person, no sin could be less pardonable; had they been convinced that this was the Messiah they would never have crucified him — but they did not permit themselves to receive conviction. Ellicott finds Peter's handling of ignorance in exact agreement with Paul's: men were ignorant where they might have known, had they not let prejudice overpower reason and conscience, so that their ignorance was not invincible and had to be repented of — yet because it was ignorance, repentance remained possible. Robertson sums it up in Hackett's phrase: they had sinned, but their sin was not of so deep a dye that it could not have been more heinous still.

That the whole had been foretold is the last stroke, handled as comfort rather than excuse. Barnes is emphatic that the prediction changed nothing in the act, since foreknowledge does not take away guilt, and that Peter urges it not to acquit them but to show that, the death being part of a plan for opening pardon, there was mercy to be had. He calls it a signal instance of God overruling wicked conduct to his own purposes, while the sinner gets no credit from an outcome he never intended. Clarke says the same more briefly, that their ignorance and malice were overruled by the wisdom of God and became instruments of fulfilling his purpose, and that all the prophets had declared it, some in express terms and others by symbol, the whole Mosaic dispensation referring to Christ. Robertson calls this the immense paradox — that their crime, real as it was, carried out the purpose of God — a stumbling block to those hearers as it still is. Calvin puts comfort and caution together: ignorance made them guilty, yet God brought to pass what he had determined, that Christ should redeem them by his death; our evils are turned by his counsel to another end than we intended, which is no excuse, since so far as in us lies we destroy ourselves by sinning.
19:
The second imperative has been badly served by the English, and Barnes says so at length. To be converted conveys an idea not in the original, that of passivity, as though the hearers were to yield to some outside influence; whereas the word means to turn, to return to a path one has strayed from, and then to turn away from sins. Repent and turn would be better, since being converted cannot well be made a matter of obligation, while turning to God is the duty of every sinner. Ellicott notes that the word is characteristic of this book, occurring eleven times and, with one exception, always in its higher spiritual sense, and that the middle voice gives it the force of the older prophets' call to turn yourselves. Wesley makes the same complaint from the other end: the term, common as it is in modern writings, very rarely occurs in Scripture, and perhaps not once in the sense we now give it. Gill notes only that the Ethiopic version adds, and be baptized.

What blotting out means is drawn from three practices. Barnes takes it from creditors cancelling a debt, and more exactly from writing on tablets covered with wax and then inverting the stylus to smooth the wax again, so that every trace of the record disappears — which expresses forgiveness better than blotting does. Sin cannot be pardoned before a man repents of it, so that in the work of grace repentance always precedes pardon. Clarke looks instead to the ceremony of the waters of jealousy, where the curse written in the book was blotted out with the bitter water, and presses it home: these men had said, his blood be upon us, so that their sins stood written against them and cried for punishment, and only that same blood could save them. Calvin observes that in exhorting to repentance Peter also declares that remission is prepared before the face of God, since no man can be stirred to repent unless salvation is set before him, and one who despairs of pardon runs headlong against God without fear. This is why, he says, the Papists cannot deliver the doctrine of repentance: they talk much of it, but having overthrown the hope of grace they leave the soul in doubt. Henry states the necessity plainly, that repentance must be solemnly charged on the conscience of everyone who desires his sins blotted out.

The clause about the times of refreshing turns on a Greek particle, and most think the Authorised Version has it wrong. Ellicott is flattest: the conjunction never has the force of when, and the sense is, that so the times of refreshing may come — a thought found in both apostles, that the conversion of sinners, and of Israel especially, hastens the fulfilment of God's purposes. Clarke reports Lightfoot contending for the same rendering, and Robertson says flatly that it is not when. Barnes lays out the two parties, Kuinoel, Grotius and the Syriac on one side, Calvin, Beza and the Vulgate on the other, and grants that the construction admits either; but he objects that it is hard to see how the repentance of these hearers should introduce the times of refreshing, and that this hardly suits a discourse meant to assure them that pardon might now be had. On what the refreshing is, Clarke offers a respite or breathing time, either the interval before the destruction of Jerusalem, given them to repent in, or the whole reign of the kingdom of grace. Ellicott takes the word as unique in the New Testament, and distinguishes these seasons from the restitution that follows, calling them its gracious preludes, when the weary are quickened as by the fresh breeze of morning — and adds the sequel, that Israel as a nation did not repent, so that hatred and strife went on to the bitter end without refreshment.
20:
A textual question stands at the head of this verse, and they are unusually united about it. Barnes reports that a large majority of manuscripts read appointed where the received text reads preached, a reading approved by Griesbach, Knapp and Bengel and followed by the ancient Syriac, and he calls it undoubtedly the true one. Clarke lists the same witnesses more fully, the chief uncials with fifty other copies, the Syriac, the Arabic and Chrysostom, and draws the point out of it: Christ crucified was the person God had from the beginning appointed for that people, so that what they were to expect was not a triumphant Messiah but one who must suffer and die. Ellicott gives the better reading in a line, which was fore-appointed for you. Robertson agrees, deriving the word from a root meaning ready to hand, so that it carries the sense of choosing; and he notes that the order is not Jesus Christ nor Christ Jesus but the Messiah, Jesus, which identifies the one with the other.

Which sending is meant divides them sharply. Gill argues that neither coming will fit. It cannot be the first, since Christ had been sent and was gone, which would leave the awakened hearers no hope after what they had done; and it cannot be the second, since they could only conclude he was coming to take vengeance, and would look on him whom they had pierced with horror. What is meant, he says, is a sending in the ministration of the word and by his Spirit, to the comfort of their souls. Clarke reads it much the same way, that on believing in the one who suffered for their sins he would be sent again in the power of his Spirit to justify and save them. Robertson takes the opposite view, that the reference is naturally to the second coming, as the next verse shows, though he allows with Knowling a spiritual presence of the enthroned Jesus which believers enjoy as a foretaste, and that repentance helps get the world ready for the King. Wesley states it briefly, that the apostles generally speak of the second coming as just at hand. Barnes puts the whole under one economy: the Messiah is to be sent to teach, to redeem, to judge and to gather his people, which is itself the argument for repenting, that they might escape in the day of judgment.

Calvin makes the mention of judgment the engine of the exhortation. He prefers Beza's rendering to the elliptical construction of the older interpreters, and reads it thus: sins are forgiven against the day of the last judgment, since unless we are cited before God's judgment-seat we are not careful to pacify him. Nothing pricks men more than being taught that they must give an account, for while our senses are held fast in this world they lie drowned in a lethargy, and the message of the last judgment must sound like a trumpet before we are truly awake. He finds two spurs in it. The profit of faith does not appear in this world, where it often goes well with the despisers of God while the life of the godly is full of miseries, so that our hearts would faint if we did not remember a day of rest coming; and the fearful judgment shakes off delicacy besides. Peter therefore mixes threatenings with promises, partly to allure and partly to drive, and makes the day of Christ a thing his hearers may desire rather than dread — while saying expressly that Christ shall be the Judge, so that contempt of the gospel may be known to be punishable, which also comforts the faithful, since salvation lies in the hand of the one who now offers it. By adding that the Judge is he who is preached to them now, Peter takes away every excuse of ignorance.
21:
That heaven should hold the Messiah was the hardest saying for such hearers. Barnes explains why: the common Jewish belief was that the Messiah would reign on earth for ever, so his absence was an objection against him, and the apostles had to establish the ascension, their evidence being that they had watched it. The word rendered must means that it was fit or proper, that he might direct the affairs of the universe for the church and exercise there his office of intercession; and Barnes thinks it remarkable that Peter cited no text for it. Ellicott gives the verb a pregnant force: receive and hold. Gill takes it either way — heaven holds and retains him in his human nature, which does not hinder his coming meanwhile to his people spiritually, or else he must receive heaven and reign there. Calvin notices the same ambiguity and refuses to settle it: the words may mean that Christ is comprehended in the heavens or that he comprehends them, and since the expression is doubtful we should hold to what is certain, that Christ is to be sought nowhere but in heaven. These hearers might have believed him risen without knowing where; Peter tells them, so that they may lift their minds high and seek him by faith.

The word rendered restitution is rare enough to be argued over. Barnes takes the verb from its use for restoring a sprained limb, notes its use in Josephus for the return from Babylon, and presses a second sense found in Philo, that of consummation or filling up, which the Syriac and Arabic versions adopt: until the complement of the times, that is, of all that the prophets foretold. He is careful about the limit: all things means all the prophets spoke, and does not mean that all men shall be saved or that every evil of sin can be repaired — the mischief is done and cannot be undone. Robertson adds that the papyri use it for repairs to temples, and that as a medical term it means restoration to health. Clarke and Ellicott prefer restoration to an earlier and better state. Clarke gets it from the prefix, which implies that the good state now settled was preceded by a bad one, and applies it to the reign of grace, wrought in every believing soul and at last universally. Ellicott finds a parallel in the promise of new heavens and a new earth, denies that the word necessarily involves the salvation of all men, and yet holds that it expresses a state in which righteousness rather than sin has dominion — which suggests a wider hope of growth in holiness, or even of repentance, in the unseen world than Christendom has been content with.

What remains is the interval. Calvin distinguishes force from effect: Christ has already restored all things by his death, but the effect does not yet appear, the restoring being still in course while we groan under the burden of servitude, the kingdom only begun and its perfection deferred to the last day. If we see much confusion in the world, this hope should set us on our feet; Christ does not appear at once because the warfare of the Church is not yet complete, its term appointed by God and not ours to anticipate. Wesley reads the phrase as comprising the whole course of New Testament times between the ascension and the coming in glory, the most eminent being the apostolic age and the spotless Church. Ellicott finds in the clause about the prophets a compact statement of doctrine: they spoke as they were moved, and he who spoke by them was nothing less than God. Clarke notes that the word all is absent from the chief manuscripts, and offers two readings of the last phrase — from the giving of the law, or from the foundation of the world.
22:
Why Moses is cited rather than a plainer prophecy is the first question. Barnes answers from the aim of the sermon: the authority of Moses was absolute, so it mattered to show that they were not departing from his law but that he had foretold this; and since Peter's object was to fix their guilt, he sets their obligation to obey before them by the command that whoever would not hear such a prophet should be cut off — so that in putting him to death they violated their own lawgiver. Calvin makes the same defence from the other side, that Peter thereby proves he is not making them revolt from Moses, since obeying this chief teacher is itself part of the law. He grants that plainer testimonies lay to hand, and explains the choice: what is in question is the authority of the teaching, and Peter would have preached all else in vain unless they were first persuaded that this teacher must be reverently heard. Henry calls it a powerful stroke to warn them of unbelief in the words of their favourite prophet, out of pretended zeal for whom they were ready to reject Christianity. Clarke draws it further: Christ came not as an ordinary prophet exhorting to amendment but as a legislator giving a new law, so that the gospel supersedes the old.

Whether the promise means one prophet or a succession is disputed, and the two who argue it fullest agree. Barnes reads the passage in its context, where Moses warns the people against the enchanters of surrounding nations and assures them that the Lord will raise up a prophet from time to time to guide them instead; so understood, the promise pertains to the series of prophets and has no direct reference to the Messiah, except as he was one of that series. Peter's appeal rests on the Messiah sustaining the character of a prophet, on the words applying to him by eminence, and on this being such an emergency as the promise contemplated. Calvin argues at greater length and will go no further. The context shows that Moses does not speak of one man only, and those who catch at the phrase about likeness press it too hard; there is no cause, he says, why we should be laughed at by the Jews for wresting the words, as if Moses spoke of Christ alone. Yet the citation is fit, since what appertains to the other prophets chiefly commends Christ, the one toward whom every former prophecy was directed, and by whose mouth God at last spoke absolutely. Ellicott admits the earlier prophets as partial fulfilments, while observing that the words had fixed men's minds on one great prophet excelling all others, as the question put to the Baptist shows; none between Moses and Jesus had marked a new epoch. Robertson notes that Moses claims to have been raised up a prophet himself, and that a greater would follow.

What the likeness consists in Wesley sets out most fully. Moses instituted the Jewish Church and Christ the Christian; with the prophesying of Moses was joined the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt, and with Christ's the deliverance of his people from sin and death; Moses spoke only what God commanded, and so did Christ — yet though like Moses he was infinitely superior in person and office. Cyril takes the phrase as a question of chronology, asking when this expected prophet came and answering from Jacob's blessing on Judah, that a ruler should not fail out of Judah until he come for whom it is reserved; the cessation of the Jewish rule was the sign of the advent. Ellicott notices that the clause about hearing him in all things is a parenthesis, suggesting a quotation from memory. Gill notes that the words about the fathers are absent from the Latin and Syriac and the Alexandrian copy.
23:
The threat attached to the promise is not quoted word for word, and the close readers say so. Barnes points out that the verb here is not the usual one for coming to pass but carries the sense of obligation, and that the sentence gives the meaning of the older passage rather than its letter: the Hebrew reads that God will require it of the man, which the Greek version turns into taking vengeance, without specifying how. The customary mode of punishing such offences was cutting the offender off from among the people, and though the word chosen here properly means to exterminate, to be destroyed from among a people meant excommunication — the loss of sacrifice, of worship, of standing, so that a man was reckoned a heathen and an outcast, which was probably the severest penalty the nation knew. Ellicott agrees that the substituted words echo a phrase familiar from Exodus and Leviticus, and takes this for another free citation. Robertson notes the emphatic form of that prophet and the symmetry behind it, that the people had refused to hearken to Moses and many were now refusing to hearken to Christ; the verb for destroying utterly is late, found here alone in the New Testament though common in the Greek Old Testament. Gill glosses the subject simply as every person, man or woman.

What such a penalty establishes is Calvin's subject. The authority of all the prophets, and most of all of Christ, is settled by this grievous punishment of the rebellious, and for good reason: since God accounts nothing more precious than his word, he cannot suffer it to be contemned, and under the law a man who despised it was adjudged to die. Calvin reads the phrase about being put away from among the people against the adoption of Abraham's stock, made on the terms that simply to be numbered among them should be their chief felicity — blessed is the people whose God is the Lord. It follows that whoever refuses to hear Christ is blotted out of the book of life, since no man is worthy to be counted of the Church who refuses the Master by whom God teaches, and a man who will not be under the Head cuts himself off from the body. Wesley admires the construction of the appeal: one cannot imagine a more masterly warning to the Jews of the consequence of their unbelief, made in the very words of their favourite prophet, out of a pretended zeal for whom they had rejected Christ. Barnes turns it on the hearers, that in crucifying Jesus they had exposed themselves to the severest punishment their law knew, and had all the more reason to repent.

Why the roll of witnesses begins at Samuel is asked by four, and answered much alike. Barnes supposes he is named because he was the first prophet after Moses to record a prediction touching the Messiah, since the Jews counted Joshua the first of the prophets but neither Joshua nor Judges contains a distinct one; from Moses to Samuel probably no prophet arose, God being consulted instead by Urim and Thummim. Clarke reports Lightfoot to the same effect, that Moses and Samuel are coupled here as in the Psalm because there were few or no prophets between them, the appearance of angels having been commoner, and that after the death of Phinehas it is doubtful whether the oracle by Urim and Thummim continued till Samuel's time. Gill adds the Jewish titles for him, master of the prophets and first in the chain of tradition, and observes that few prophets stood between him and Moses where many followed after, the schools having been set up in his days. Ellicott gives both reasons, that Samuel founded those schools and so represents the whole goodly fellowship, and that he uttered one of the earliest predictions reckoned distinctively Messianic.
25:
What it means to be sons of the prophets is not agreed. Barnes takes it as discipleship rather than descent: they were not the literal posterity of the prophets but their pupils, since teachers among the Jews were commonly called fathers and their disciples sons — and as professed disciples they were bound to listen. Gill takes it the other way, of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who are themselves called prophets, so that these hearers were lineally and naturally descended from the men to whom the promises of the Messiah belonged, and were their heirs. Clarke makes the phrase an argument aimed at the men themselves: as children or disciples of the prophets they were bound to believe their predictions and obey their precepts, and were entitled to their promises, so that duty and interest went hand in hand. Wesley says the same in a line, that as the first heirs the prophecies and the covenant belong to them properly.

The second title needs a definition, and Barnes supplies a careful one. A covenant properly means a compact between parties who have a right to choose or refuse the terms; applied to God and man it means a firm promise on God's part, to be regarded with all the sacredness of a compact, and is called a covenant only to mark that sacredness and the certainty of its fulfilment — for since man has no right to reject any of the terms, there has strictly been no compact between them at all. Robertson notes that the Greek says literally the covenant which God covenanted, the noun and the verb being of one root, and that the same word does duty for covenant and for will in the letter to the Hebrews. Ellicott finds in the choice of the Abrahamic covenant a mark of the unity of apostolic teaching, since Peter rests on it with as full an emphasis as Paul does after learning that it implicitly involved the calling of the Gentiles. Barnes adds that the word rendered kindreds means those who have a common ancestor, applied to families and then to whole nations, and that it plainly means all nations here.

Calvin builds a doctrine of the covenanted family on the verse. The grace of the covenant, he says, was appointed principally for these hearers, and Peter, having pricked them forward with the terror of punishment, now allures them with the grace offered in Christ — it being a wise minister's duty to prick forward the sluggish and lead gently those apt to be taught. He presses the necessity of that particular application: it is not enough that mercy be preached generally, since a man who thought the gospel had come by chance would have a wavering opinion instead of faith, and God does not cast forth uncertain voices to hang in the air but directs them to us by his determinate counsel. The argument itself he states as a syllogism — God made his covenant with our fathers, therefore we their posterity are comprehended in it — and turns it against those who expound the children of Abraham only allegorically, as though God had no respect to the stock when he promised to be the God of Abraham's seed. Peter is not speaking of the shadows of the law, Calvin insists, but affirming that under the kingdom of Christ God adopts the children with the fathers, so that the grace of salvation reaches those not yet born. He grants the objection, that many children of the faithful according to the flesh are counted bastards, having thrust themselves out of the holy progeny by unbelief; but this does not hinder the Lord from admitting the seed of the godly into the fellowship of grace, and though the common election is not effectual in all, it may set open a gate for the special elect.
26:
The word first is loaded, and everyone remarks on it. Barnes takes it for the rule that the gospel should be preached to the Jews before others, beginning at Jerusalem, and notes that Jesus himself had confined his ministry to them. Robertson puts the reason in a sentence: the Jews were first in privilege, and through them the Messiah was to come for all the families of the earth. Clarke ties it to the previous verse, that as children of the prophets and of the covenant the first offers of salvation belonged to them by right. Ellicott hears in the turn of the phrase an agreement with Paul's formula about the Jew first and also the Gentile, and draws an inference: Peter does not yet know on what conditions the gospel will be preached to the heathen, but the word implies a distinct perception that there was a call to preach to them at all.

What the raising up means is disputed, as earlier in the chapter. Barnes denies that it refers to the resurrection, taking it in the sense the words of Moses had borne, where God promised to raise up a prophet and send him — so that Peter means God had commissioned his Son to preach and turn men from their sins. Gill allows either reading, since the phrase is sometimes used of the incarnation and the manifestation of Christ in human nature, and sometimes of the resurrection and the exaltation at God's right hand. Calvin declines the rendering of Erasmus, which speaks of a thing done long ago, and holds instead that Christ was raised up when he was declared to be the author of the blessing — a thing done lately and suddenly, which ought to have moved these hearers the more. To raise up a prophet, he explains, is to furnish him with the gifts his office needs and prefer him to the degree of prophetical honour; Christ was so raised when he fulfilled the function his Father enjoined, and the same is done daily whenever he is offered in the gospel. Ellicott notes a nicety of the Greek, that the participle is present where the English gives an infinitive, so that Christ is sent as in the act of blessing.

The last clause defines the blessing, and none will let it be softened. Ellicott is the most exact: the verb which commonly means a spoken benediction is here used for the reality of blessedness, and the blessing is found not in exemption from punishment, nor even in pardon, but in a change of heart, in turning each man from his wickednesses — the plural implying all the forms wickedness can take. Barnes says the same more broadly, that the highest blessing which can be conferred on men is to be turned from sin, the source of all their woes, and that Christ blesses nobody in sin but only by turning him out of it. Clarke draws two conclusions and presses them hard. The salvation promised in the covenant was from sin and not from the Romans, and no man has his sin blotted out who does not turn from it; and neither political nor ecclesiastical privilege benefits the soul by itself, since a man may have Abraham for his father according to the flesh and Satan for his father according to the spirit — for if he is not turned from his iniquities, even the death of Christ profits him nothing. Calvin makes it a caution about the order of benefits: Christ does not do away the sins of the faithful so that they may take licence to sin under that colour, but makes them new men at the same time, as Isaiah promises a Redeemer to Zion and then adds the reservation, to those in Jacob who turn from their iniquities. Wesley closes the chapter by calling this the great gospel blessing.
